name: binwalk
one_line: search a binary file for embedded files and executable code
plain: `binwalk` scans a file for other files hidden inside it. Many files are really containers: a firmware image holds a filesystem, a kernel and compressed blobs; a picture can have a ZIP glued on its end; a PDF can hold scripts.

It looks for magic numbers (the signature bytes that start a ZIP, PNG, gzip, ELF...), prints each hit with its offset, and can carve the pieces out into folders. It can also measure entropy: very random data is usually encrypted or compressed, plain data is not.
In CTFs it answers 'is there something inside this file?' in seconds.
when: A challenge image or file seems larger than it should be.
Look inside a router or IoT firmware image.
Extract an appended archive from a picture.
Find which parts of a file are compressed or encrypted (entropy).
Disassemble-guess a blob of code to see its CPU type.

examples.title: Scan a file for hidden content
examples.explain: Prints a table of DECIMAL offset, HEX offset and DESCRIPTION. A second hit such as 'Zip archive data' at a large offset means a ZIP is appended to the picture.

examples.title: Extract everything it finds
examples.explain: -e carves the pieces out into a folder named _mystery.jpg.extracted. Needs helper tools such as unzip or 7z installed.

examples.title: Extract and unpack recursively
examples.explain: -M follows the extraction: contents of contents are scanned again, as in firmware that contains a filesystem that contains archives.

examples.title: Draw an entropy graph
examples.explain: -E calculates entropy and plots it. A flat line near 1.0 is encrypted or compressed; low and varied is ordinary data. Use -N to skip the plot window.

examples.title: Look for CPU code
examples.explain: -A searches for common instruction patterns (ARM, MIPS, x86...), useful when you do not know the architecture.

examples.title: Scan only for certain signatures
examples.explain: -y keeps only these signature types, so a noisy file gives a short list.

examples.title: Skip noisy signatures
examples.explain: -x excludes types that produce lots of false hits.

examples.title: Show raw text hits
examples.explain: -R searches for your own byte sequence (here the ZIP header PK\x03\x04) and prints each offset.

examples.title: Carve by hand with dd
examples.explain: Binwalk gave you an offset (48210). dd copies from there to a new file. Great when automatic extraction fails.

examples.title: Analyse many files
examples.explain: -r keeps going through a list of files and writes a short summary for each.

mistakes: Running -e as root on an untrusted file: extraction can follow malicious symlinks. Run it as a normal user in a throw-away folder.
Taking every hit as real: many 'matches' are false positives. Check the offset and the size.
Missing the extraction tools (unzip, 7z, sasquatch, jefferson): binwalk then finds but cannot extract.
Forgetting -M for nested containers: you only get the first layer.
Not looking at the end of the file: use tail -c and xxd as well.
try: Append a zip to a picture with cat pic.jpg secret.zip > both.jpg, then find it with binwalk both.jpg.
Extract it with -e and read the result.
Run binwalk -E on a ZIP and on a text file and compare the entropy.
Use dd with an offset binwalk reports to carve a part by hand.
